title: SE201 Lesson 4: Parallel agents, one integration

scenes.text: Quick question. Three agents each build one part of a system. All three say, done. All three pass their own checks. Is the system done? [pause] Yes? Almost? Or does nobody know yet? [pause] <emphasis>Nobody knows yet.</emphasis> Each check proves one part works alone. Not one of them has seen the parts together.

data.question:
Three agents. Three parts. Every part
passes its own check. Is the system done?
data.why:
No check has
seen the parts
together.

scenes.text: Picture a team that splits one feature across three agents. One builds the screen. One builds the service behind it. One changes the database. Each part gets finished, and each part is correct on its own. [pause] Then the parts meet. The screen asks for a field the service never sends. Two of the agents edited the same file. And nobody finds out until the very end, when it costs the most to fix.

data.label: PICTURE A TEAM  ·  ONE FEATURE, THREE AGENTS, NO PLAN FOR THE MERGE
data.caption: Every part passed. The system didn’t.

scenes.text: Parallel work is only fast if it comes back together cleanly. So plan the integration <emphasis>first</emphasis>. Before any agent starts.

data.headline:
Plan the integration first.
Before any agent starts.

scenes.text: Three things. First, a shared contract. Write down what crosses between the parts: the interfaces, the formats, the names, and who owns which files. At enterprise scale, that's an A.P.I., or a schema. It can be one page. But it has to exist before the work starts. And when it has to change, change it in one place, where every agent sees it.

data.label: THE PLAN FOR COMING BACK TOGETHER

contract.text:
Interfaces
Formats, names
Who owns
which files

data.caption: First: write down what crosses, before the work starts.

scenes.text: Then every agent gets its own brief, its own finish line, and its own check. And part of that check is: does it match the contract?

data.label: THE PLAN FOR COMING BACK TOGETHER

contract.text:
Interfaces
Formats, names
Who owns
which files

data.caption: Each agent: its own brief, its own finish line, its own check.

scenes.text: Second, one merge point. One place where the parts come together. So when something doesn't fit, there's exactly one place to look. And use it early. Join rough versions of the parts on day one. Don't let the first meeting be the last step.

data.label: THE PLAN FOR COMING BACK TOGETHER

contract.text:
Interfaces
Formats, names
Who owns
which files

data.caption: Second: one place where the parts meet. Early.

scenes.text: Third, test the whole system. Not just each part. The assembled thing, running as one. That's the check no single agent could run alone.

data.label: THE PLAN FOR COMING BACK TOGETHER

contract.text:

data.caption: Third: test the whole, not just each part.

scenes.text: Here's a real one. Lessons three, four and five of software engineering one oh one were built at the same time. Three scripts, three renders, running side by side. The three finished videos landed within forty seconds of each other.

data.label: A REAL ONE  ·  SOFTWARE ENGINEERING 101, LESSONS 3 TO 5
data.caption:

same time.
Done within

scenes.text: And they came back together in one place. The contract already existed: the same script format the first two lessons used, and the same page fields. One merge point: one content file, read by one generator that builds every page. And they shipped together, in one change. [pause] Today that path has two more gates. One check that walks the whole site: every link, and every file a page points to. And a pull request to staging, for me to approve. [pause] This lesson and the one before it were drafted in parallel, too.

data.label: HOW THE THREE LESSONS CAME BACK TOGETHER  ·  PLUS TODAY’S GATES

scenes.text: Parallel isn't free. You pay for it at the merge. With the integration planned first, three agents finish sooner than one working down a list. Without a plan, the time you saved comes back as rework. [pause] And if two parts keep needing each other's answers, they aren't parallel work. Go back to the graph.

data.label: THREE AGENTS, TWO WAYS  ·  AN ILLUSTRATION, NOT A MEASUREMENT

bars.name: No plan for the merge: build fast, then rework

data.note: The time is won or lost at the merge.
data.fine: IF TWO PARTS KEEP NEEDING EACH OTHER, GO BACK TO THE GRAPH

scenes.text: So, to recap. Split only where nothing crosses. Agree the contract before anyone starts. Merge early, in one place. And test the whole, not just the parts.

data.headline: Parallel agents, one integration
items: Agree the contract before anyone starts
Test the whole, not just the parts

scenes.text: Which gives us rule four, for your agents. Before you run agents in parallel, plan how the work comes back together. Write the shared contract first. Give each agent its own brief, its own finish line, and its own check. Merge early, in one place. And test the whole system, not just each part.

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Think of the last time work was split, across agents, or across people. Where did the parts first meet? [pause] And who checked the whole thing?
